title: The #1 Dating Rule That Saves You Months of Heartbreak
guest: Sabrina Zohar, dating and relationship coach, host of The Sabrina Zohar Show
summary: Dating coach Sabrina Zohar joins the sisters to argue that healthy dating starts with nervous-system self-regulation, boundaries and refusing to self-abandon, not with tactics. She gives concrete tools (the pause, sour candy, ice, 'how old do I feel?'), a script for co-regulating with a partner, a framework for grieving relationships that end when you set boundaries, and a critique of outcome-driven internet dating gurus. The hosts share their own friendship-breakup and 'I'm too much' struggles.

ideas.idea: Self-regulation of your nervous system is the crux of being in a healthy, secure relationship, because the nervous system is the lens through which you see and handle everything.
ideas.detail: Sabrina describes waking seven times a night checking for texts; a text meant she could breathe, no text felt like the end of the world. Conflict-repair should really be conflict-regulate-repair, since a dysregulated body thinks there is a tiger when it is really just a phone.

ideas.idea: Love yourself more than you need to be loved by others, so that you are OK walking away, saying no, and choosing rather than needing a partner.
ideas.detail: Her mother's saying; most online dating advice is about self-abandonment (how do I get you to like/validate/choose me), and if you are doing that you have already lost yourself.

ideas.idea: The number one tool for anxiety is the 'power of the pause': put one minute between stimulus and response so you respond instead of react.
ideas.detail: Knowing the theory is like knowing how to deadlift intellectually; you still need to practice the implementation. The pause is step one before any regulation technique.

ideas.idea: Regulating the nervous system means signaling to your body you are not in immediate danger, and practical tools include walking, shaking, the 'silent punch', ice cubes and sour candy.
ideas.detail: Intense cold triggers the mammalian dive response and the parasympathetic nervous system; sour candy works because the brain cannot ruminate and process a strong stimulus at once, which turns the prefrontal cortex back on. She uses the analogy of an office building where the executives (prefrontal cortex) go offline and children run the show; humming and Wim Hof breathwork also activate the vagus nerve. Meditation is useless when you are dysregulated because you must feel safe first.

ideas.idea: When triggered, ask 'how old do I feel and where did I learn this?' because the reaction is usually a childhood core belief projected onto the other person, not about them.
ideas.detail: When someone doesn't text back and 'the pinch doesn't match the ouch', you rarely feel like a 35-year-old; you feel seven, and it's your dad. This gives you agency and reveals that you hyper-fixate on people who don't offer clarity because it gives you dopamine. Her book on patterns, 'Why Am I Like This?', comes out in October.

ideas.idea: Showing yourself self-compassion releases more dopamine than external validation, so validating your own feelings closes the loop in your brain instead of waiting for someone else.
ideas.detail: Saying 'given everything I've been through, no wonder this makes me feel this way' gives the brain finality, and the hosts note it breaks the cycle of needing the text back.

ideas.idea: The difference between intuition and anxiety is urgency: intuition is calm and immediate, anxiety is frantic and urgent.
ideas.detail: Fear responses are fight, flight, freeze and fawn (and anxious people can be avoidant too). 'Why haven't they called me' is urgency; a secure response is 'they're at work, I'll hear later' without assuming ill intent.

ideas.idea: Co-regulate with a partner by first regulating yourself, then asking consent to share, and using I-statements to explain the trigger rather than projecting onto them.
ideas.detail: When her partner Ryan said 'no' to an outing, she spiraled, realized she felt seven and it was her dismissive father, then said 'when you said no I shut down; it reminded me of my dad; could you share your why so I don't feel alone on an island.' They have never had that issue since.

ideas.idea: Growth requires learning to grieve, because people who benefited from your lack of boundaries will be threatened when you start setting them.
ideas.detail: Expanding your 'window of tolerance' (how much you can handle before hyper-arousal or shutdown) means having uncomfortable conversations and accepting that some friendships have run their course. She notes she once 'married her father' in a toxic relationship and got out by learning to say no.

ideas.idea: Boundaries don't keep people out, they protect what's in; they are for you, and no one can cross your boundary, only reveal whether they respect it.
ideas.detail: A match who mocked her 'let's meet in person, no endless app chat' preference as 'rushing to the altar' didn't cross her boundary, he showed he didn't respect it. If you don't take calls after 9, someone calling doesn't cross the boundary; you cross your own by answering. A DBT practice: think of 'future you' when setting the boundary.

ideas.idea: Boundaries should be flexible rather than rigid, and setting them means being OK with disappointing people, judged by whether you are being hurtful or harmful.
ideas.detail: Declining lunch because of a big meeting may hurt feelings; refusing to drive a friend to surgery for a self-care day is harmful. You can afford to hurt feelings, not to harm.

ideas.idea: Difficulty with boundaries usually traces back to childhood, including 'little t' traumas, not only big traumas.
ideas.detail: Growing up in a narcissistic household where the narcissist is the sun and everyone orbits them, saying no meant being hit or alienated, so she learned 'play quiet and they'll love you', which is maladaptive as an adult. A mother working full time and being absent is a little-t trauma that still leaves a mark without the parents being bad.

ideas.idea: How people respond when you set a boundary is deeply revealing; if they are offended rather than just disappointed, maybe they aren't meant to be in your life.
ideas.detail: Jean, at 30 and in her 'Saturn return', has been setting boundaries in friendships over the past year and a half. Sabrina ended a ten-year codependent friendship after a 14-hour shoot day when the friend replied 'you wasted my time' to her saying she needed to go home early, and says she has never been better.

ideas.idea: You won't feel better until you feel; an emotion takes about 90 seconds to run its course if you sit with it instead of shaming and blaming yourself for it.
ideas.detail: Describe the feeling's color, shape and texture and it dissipates. The brain loves to finish things, so if you don't create your own closure it will hyper-fixate until it gets one. Feeling bad about feeling bad ('I should be over it') is shame learned from survival tactics.

ideas.idea: Grieve by doing inner-child work: speak to your younger self with the compassion adults didn't give you, telling her it was never her job to make people happy.
ideas.detail: Sabrina walks Cherie through this live, and posts a photo of 'little me' on Instagram daily to reconnect. Attacking yourself with 'you should have known better' is talking to a six-year-old the way adults once did.

ideas.idea: 'I should have seen this coming' is the illusion of control, learned as childhood hypervigilance, and the social consequences you fear from walking away usually never materialize.
ideas.detail: Cherie describes a traumatic friendship breakup a year ago with a friend she treated like a sister who couldn't accept her boundary; she stayed too long to avoid rocking friend-group boats, but after ending it none of the feared consequences happened and she feels better. 'If me saying something pushes you away, I never had you to begin with.'

ideas.idea: Enter new relationships with boundaries already set and make people earn their place rather than handing over 'the keys to the castle' because they say it's a pretty house.
ideas.detail: Frame past patterns as 'what did I used to accept that I'm no longer willing to' and take accountability without shame: 'I allowed it, maybe out of trauma or attachment, and now I choose differently.'

ideas.idea: If you feel 'too much' in dating, you are usually with people who lack bandwidth or are emotionally unavailable; if I'm too much, go find less.
ideas.detail: Using IFS 'fusion' language: you have anxious attachment, you are not it; ask who taught you that you're too much. Her father had no patience for her emotions, but her partner thinks she is 'just enough' because she stopped shrinking. Cherie relates via feeling like a burden, which traces to a 6-7 year old raised by a single mother without bandwidth.

ideas.idea: Self-abandonment is saying yes when you want to say no, and society teaches women in particular to stay small; if you don't stand for something you fall for everything.
ideas.detail: Every woman she has met has said yes instead of no in some sexual, professional or personal context. Even 'go kiss your uncle' teaches kids they have no choice, but as an adult you do. Rewiring takes repetition and 'small micro yeses' (she has to do 3 breaths and say 'I'm safe' before every meal due to blood-sugar issues from dysregulation).

ideas.idea: Date (and do business) with detachment: detach from the outcome, not from your feelings, controlling only what you can and surrendering the rest.
ideas.detail: She has done nine years of daily work and is not done: 'if this is it, I don't want it.' You can't control other people, only yourself.

ideas.idea: You should always be in your growth stage and can reinvent yourself at any time; if you can't let go, life will be very hard.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she is a totally different person than 18 months ago; two years ago she was a 'corporate girly' running a product at Snapchat and would never have believed podcasting would be her main job.

ideas.idea: When life collapses you can choose to be the phoenix and treat it as happening for you, not to you, finding meaning through ACT rather than 'everything happens for a reason'.
ideas.detail: Sabrina owned a clothing company and was on the Shark Tank set about to pitch Mark Cuban when she was sent home, then again a month later, then her dog died a month after that; she rebuilt as a dating coach via TikTok. Growth shows in small moments like not freaking out when a guy cuts you off.

ideas.idea: You are not a snowflake: everyone shares the same core fears ('is there something wrong with me, do I belong, am I too much'), and that makes you human, not broken.
ideas.detail: She prefers 'a longer table, not a higher fence'; being on an island is what makes you feel alone.

ideas.idea: Internet dating gurus like 'if he wanted to, he would', 'sprinkle sprinkle' and 'daddy academies' are outcome-driven formulas that teach self-abandonment and keep people single longer.
ideas.detail: Business works as 'do X get Y' but relationships don't; want and do are different parts of the brain. She blocked a creator who called her advice 'low value' for endorsing coffee dates; she argues a 30-minute coffee respects her time more than a 2-3 hour dinner with a stranger, and worth comes from morals and ethics, not whether it's dinner or drinks. Gurus give formulaic behaviors without teaching the underlying value system.
names_or_cases: if he wanted to, he would

ideas.idea: Trying to control another person's actions or the outcome never works; a strong relationship is two self-healed pillars communicating effectively.
ideas.detail: Sabrina broke every 'rule' with her partner (slept together the first night) but told him plainly 'I don't do casual; if you call it's because you want to build something, don't waste my time.' He later said he loved that she wasn't afraid to lose him, only afraid of losing herself. They make a conscious choice to choose each other every day.
